## Study objective

The thesis tests whether longitudinal change in individual vocal repertoires is associated with position and relationship structure within experimentally manipulated fission–fusion social networks.

## Approach

The project combined controlled colony experiments, manual behavioural annotation, automated video capture, social-network analysis, and acoustic analysis. Network-derived predictors were related to acoustic structure at the note, motif, and sequence levels as group composition and social relationships changed.

## Scientific context

Budgerigars permit repeated measurement of learned vocal behaviour within dynamic social groups. The project addresses whether network position and changing association patterns explain vocal change beyond effects that can be estimated from isolated dyads.

## Project status

This work formed the master's thesis for my BS–MS degree at IISER Pune. I conducted the research in the [ECEB Lab](https://sites.google.com/view/eceb-lab) at JNCASR under the supervision of Anand Krishnan. No public manuscript or associated analysis package is currently linked; those outputs will be added if and when they become publicly available.
